title: File Recovery
cardText: Recover files that were deleted, moved, overwritten, corrupted or become inaccessible.
Check Recycle Bin, Trash, cloud storage, file history, snapshots and third-party backups.
Identify storage failures and use safe recovery methods without risking further data loss.
text: This guide covers missing and deleted files on Windows, macOS, external drives, network storage and cloud services.
Identify whether the file was moved, deleted, overwritten, made inaccessible or lost following a storage failure.
Check simple locations, cloud recycle bins, previous versions and backups before attempting file recovery software.
Include OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Google Drive, Dropbox and other cloud storage services where applicable.
Check Windows File History, macOS Time Machine, NAS snapshots and third-party backup software.
If accidental deletion occurred on a local drive, minimise writes to that drive immediately.
Do not run repairs, formatting or intensive scans on a suspected failing drive.
Restore recovered files to a separate location and verify their contents before replacing existing files.

identifySituation.title: Identify what happened to the file
body: Ask when the file was last seen and where it was stored.
Determine whether it was deleted, moved, renamed, overwritten, corrupted or became inaccessible.
Identify the device, operating system and storage location involved.
Check whether the file was stored on a local SSD, hard drive, USB drive, NAS or cloud service.
If the drive is missing, disconnecting, making unusual noises or reporting serious errors, investigate storage health before scanning it.
If accidental deletion is suspected, minimise writes to the affected drive while checking recovery options.

identifyOriginalLocation.title: Identify the original file location
body: Determine which folder, account, drive or application originally contained the file.
Check whether Desktop, Documents or Pictures was redirected to OneDrive or iCloud Drive.
Identify whether the file belonged to a shared folder, network drive or external device.
Check whether the user has more than one Windows, Apple, Google or Microsoft account.
Record the filename, extension, approximate size and last known modification date.
If the file was on a synchronised folder, check the cloud service before attempting disk recovery.

searchForFile.title: Search for the missing file
body: Use File Explorer search on Windows or Finder and Spotlight on macOS.
Search using the exact filename, part of the filename and file extension.
Check likely locations including Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures and recently used folders.
Check whether the file was renamed, moved into another folder or saved with a different extension.
Check the originating application's Recent Files or Open Recent list.
Search other connected drives and user profiles where appropriate.
Do not run a full-disk scan if the storage device is showing signs of physical failure.

verifyLocatedFile.title: Verify the located file
body: Check that the file has the expected name, size and modification date.
Open it in the appropriate application to confirm the contents are correct.
If multiple versions exist, identify the required version before changing anything.
Copy the verified file to a known safe location.
If the file is damaged or contains the wrong data, continue by checking versions and backups.

checkRecycleBin.title: Check Recycle Bin or Trash
body: On Windows, open Recycle Bin and search for the missing file.
On macOS, open Trash and check for the deleted file.
Use the original location and deletion date to distinguish similarly named files.
Files removed using permanent deletion, some application operations or removable storage may bypass the normal bin.
Do not empty Recycle Bin or Trash while investigating.

restoreRecycleBin.title: Restore from Recycle Bin or Trash
body: Select the required file and restore it using the operating system's restore command.
On Windows, Recycle Bin Restore normally returns the item to its original location.
On macOS, use Put Back where available.
Check that the original folder exists and that the restored file is accessible.
If a current file has the same name, avoid overwriting it until both versions have been compared.
Verify the recovered file opens and contains the expected information.

checkCloudStorage.title: Check cloud storage and synchronised folders
body: Determine whether the file was stored in OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Google Drive, Dropbox or another cloud service.
Sign in using the correct personal, work or school account.
Search the provider's website rather than relying only on the computer's synchronised folder.
Check cloud recycle bins, recently deleted files, version history and file activity.
Check whether another device moved, renamed or deleted the file through synchronisation.
For shared folders, confirm the file has not been moved or access permissions changed.
Avoid making additional bulk changes while investigating a synchronisation-related loss.

identifyCloudProvider.title: Identify the cloud storage provider
body: Check which cloud account originally held the file.
For OneDrive, use the Microsoft account or work account associated with the original folder.
For iCloud Drive, use the Apple Account associated with the device.
For Google Drive and Dropbox, verify the correct signed-in account.
Some providers retain deleted files only for a limited period, depending on account type or plan.
For business storage, administrators may have additional recovery options.

checkMicrosoftAppleCloud.title: Recover OneDrive or iCloud Drive files
body: For OneDrive, sign in at onedrive.com and open Recycle bin.
Check whether the required file appears in the cloud Recycle bin or a previous version is available.
For eligible Microsoft 365 accounts, review available OneDrive restore options if many files were affected.
For iCloud Drive, sign in at icloud.com/iclouddrive and check Recently Deleted.
Also check iCloud's Data Recovery, Restore Files option.
On a Mac, check local Trash and Time Machine for the same file.
Review the selected file before restoring and avoid overwriting a newer correct copy.
Do not assume a file can be recovered after the provider's retention period or permanent deletion.

checkOtherCloud.title: Recover Google Drive, Dropbox or other cloud files
body: For Google Drive, sign in at drive.google.com and check Trash.
Search Drive and inspect file activity for moves, renames or deletion events.
For Dropbox, sign in at dropbox.com and open Deleted files.
Check version history if the file still exists but an older version is required.
Review Dropbox Rewind where available if many files were changed or deleted.
For other services, use their official deleted-file and version-recovery procedures.
Check the provider's recovery period and the account's subscription or administration settings.
Avoid replacing a good current version without first examining the older copy.

link.description: Official Google Drive Trash recovery instructions.

link.name: Google: Find Lost Drive Files
link.description: Official help for moved, renamed, missing or shared files.

checkCloudAdminRecovery.title: Check administrator or provider recovery
body: For Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Dropbox Business or other managed accounts, contact the authorised administrator.
Ask whether retention policies, backup software, snapshots or administrator recovery tools cover the deleted file.
Check whether the file belonged to a shared drive, SharePoint library or team workspace.
For personal accounts, review the provider's official support and available recovery tools.
Do not promise recovery beyond the service's retention period.
If no cloud recovery option is available, continue checking independent backups.

restoreCloudFile.title: Restore the cloud file safely
body: Identify the correct file and version before restoring.
Use the provider's supported Restore, Recover or Download command.
If practical, download a recovered copy to a separate location before replacing a current file.
Confirm that restoration does not overwrite a newer required version.
Allow cloud synchronisation to complete.
Open the recovered file and verify its contents and attachments where applicable.
Check the file on the provider's website and in the intended local folder.

checkPreviousVersions.title: Choose the previous-version recovery method
body: Identify whether the missing file was on a Windows computer, Mac, cloud service or network storage.
For Windows, check File History and the Previous Versions tab where available.
For macOS, check Time Machine backups.
For NAS or managed network storage, check snapshots and file-version features in later backup steps.
For cloud documents, check the cloud provider’s version history in its website.
Windows System Restore is not a substitute for personal-file backup.
Choose the appropriate computer operating system; if the source is neither Windows nor macOS, continue with the backup and snapshot checks.

checkWindowsPreviousVersions.title: Check Windows File History and Previous Versions
body: Open File Explorer and browse to the original folder or its parent folder.
Right-click the folder or existing file, select Properties and open Previous Versions where available.
Look for a version from before the file was deleted or changed.
If File History was configured, search its available backed-up versions of the folder.
Use Open or preview where available to confirm the file is correct before restoring.
Prefer copying a recovered version to a separate location instead of overwriting a current file.
If no versions exist, File History or snapshots may not have been configured.

link.name: Microsoft: Restore Files with File History
link.description: Official Windows File History and previous-version recovery steps.

checkWindowsPreviousVersions.alt: Windows folder Properties dialog displaying the Previous Versions tab
checkWindowsPreviousVersions.caption: Right-click the original folder, open Properties and inspect Previous Versions before restoring a copy.

checkMacTimeMachine.title: Check macOS Time Machine or other backup versions
body: If the source computer is a Mac, connect or select the drive containing its Time Machine backups.
Open Finder and navigate to the folder where the file was previously located.
Open Time Machine and browse to a backup date when the file existed.
Preview the correct file and restore it, avoiding overwriting a newer version without a copy.
If Time Machine was not configured or no matching backup exists, check the other backup options.
If the source was Linux or network storage rather than macOS, skip Time Machine and continue to the relevant backup or NAS snapshot checks.

link.name: Apple: Restore Items with Time Machine
link.description: Official macOS Time Machine recovery instructions.

checkMacTimeMachine.alt: macOS Time Machine showing historical Finder windows for restoring an earlier file
checkMacTimeMachine.caption: Browse Time Machine backups to the date the file existed, then restore the required copy.

restorePreviousVersion.title: Restore a previous file version
body: Preview the available version and confirm that it contains the required information.
Record the date of the version being restored.
Where possible, restore to a different filename or location.
Do not overwrite an existing newer copy without preserving it first.
Open the restored file and verify its contents.
If the version is incomplete or the restore fails, continue checking other backups.

checkBackups.title: Check built-in and external backups
body: Ask whether the user has a regular computer backup.
On Windows, check File History, any existing Windows Backup configuration and legacy Backup and Restore sets.
On macOS, check Time Machine backups and any backup disks.
Check external USB drives, another computer, NAS storage and server backups.
Check whether copies were emailed, exported or saved in another application.
Confirm the backup date is old enough to contain the missing file.
Avoid connecting an untrusted or damaged drive in a way that causes automatic write operations.

checkThirdPartyBackups.title: Check third-party backup software
body: Check whether backup software was installed on the original computer, NAS or server.
Examples include Veeam, Acronis, Macrium Reflect, Backblaze, IDrive, Duplicati and other backup solutions.
Open the backup application's recovery interface and identify existing backup jobs or repositories.
Check external disks, network destinations and cloud backup accounts associated with those jobs.
Look for file-level restore, previous backup versions and deleted-file retention options.
Some backups are stored as disk images and must be mounted or browsed through the backup application.
Verify the backup set is accessible and that the required file exists before starting restoration.
For managed systems, check whether an IT administrator controls the backups.

checkNasSnapshots.title: Check NAS and network storage snapshots
body: If the file was stored on a NAS, file server or shared drive, identify the storage system.
Check whether the administrator enabled snapshots, file versioning or a network recycle bin.
For Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS or other storage platforms, use the supported snapshot or file recovery interface.
Check whether a previous version of the folder can be browsed without restoring the entire shared volume.
Do not roll back an entire shared folder or volume when only one file is missing unless the consequences are understood.
Prefer restoring the required file to a separate folder.
If the storage system is failing, stop and follow the storage-failure recovery path.

restoreBackup.title: Restore the file from backup
body: Select the correct backup date and file version.
Verify the source backup contains the required information.
Restore to a separate safe folder where possible.
Avoid replacing an existing file without first saving a copy.
Open the restored file and check its contents.
If the file came from a disk image, use the backup application's supported extraction procedure.
Keep the original backup until restoration has been confirmed.

checkRecoveryEligibility.title: Assess whether deleted-file recovery is appropriate
body: Determine whether the file was deleted from a local drive, USB device, memory card or other storage.
Check whether the drive is functioning normally and can be accessed without errors.
Record whether the storage uses an SSD, HDD, memory card or USB flash drive.
Recovery becomes less likely when deleted data has been overwritten or cleared by SSD TRIM.
Deletion age alone does not determine whether recovery is possible.
Do not install recovery software, download files or save recovered data onto the affected drive.
If the drive is physically failing, do not run a normal recovery scan; follow the storage-failure path.

prepareSoftwareRecovery.title: Prepare safe software recovery
body: Stop unnecessary use of the affected volume.
Identify the physical storage device and the partition containing the lost data.
Use another computer or a separate healthy drive for recovery tools when practical.
Prepare a separate destination drive with enough space for recovered files.
For valuable data, consider making a sector-level image before examining the source, if the drive is healthy and appropriate tools and expertise are available.
Do not create a new partition or reformat the original drive to prepare recovery space.
Do not use CHKDSK, First Aid repair or other filesystem-writing repairs as a first step when deleted-file recovery is the goal.
For SSDs, recognise that TRIM may already have made some deleted data unrecoverable.

attemptRecoverySoftware.title: Attempt deleted-file recovery software
body: Choose a reputable tool appropriate to the operating system, file system and storage device.
On Windows, consider Microsoft's Windows File Recovery for supported local storage.
Other established tools include PhotoRec and TestDisk, but they serve different recovery purposes and require care.
Run recovery against the affected source without saving recovered files to it.
Use a separate physical drive or appropriate destination for recovered data.
Check preview results where supported and select the required files.
Large scans may take considerable time; monitor drive behaviour and stop if physical failure symptoms appear.
Do not repeat scans indefinitely if no useful data is recovered.
Verify recovered files before declaring success.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows File Recovery
link.description: Official recovery tool and source/destination requirements.

link.name: CGSecurity: TestDisk and PhotoRec
link.description: Official documentation for established partition and file recovery utilities.

verifyRecoveredFile.title: Verify recovered files
body: Check that the recovered file has the expected format and plausible size.
Open it in its normal application and inspect the contents.
Confirm that any embedded images, attachments or required data are present.
Recovery tools may produce partial files, damaged files or generic filenames.
Compare the recovered content with available original information.
Save the verified copy to a safe storage location.

limitedRecovery.title: Assess remaining recovery options
body: The attempted recovery did not produce a usable file.
Check whether the drive is an SSD where TRIM may have cleared deleted data.
Review whether the original storage has been heavily used since deletion.
Check whether another backup, device or cloud version remains available.
Avoid repeated writes or aggressive recovery attempts on the affected storage.
If the data is important, professional recovery may be justified.
If the data has been overwritten or permanently cleared, recovery may not be possible.

checkDriveHealth.title: Check storage accessibility and health
body: Identify whether the drive is detected consistently by the computer.
Check for unusual clicking, repeated disconnects, slow reads, SMART warnings and input/output errors.
Check whether the issue is limited to one file or affects the entire drive.
For external drives, confirm power, cable and connection issues using safe non-destructive checks.
Avoid repeatedly powering a drive that is making abnormal mechanical noises.
If a drive is suspected of failing, preserve it before performing filesystem repairs.
A healthy drive with an inaccessible file may instead have a permissions, encryption or filesystem issue.

checkFilePermissions.title: Check permissions and encryption
body: Confirm whether the file or folder actually exists.
Check whether access is blocked by Windows NTFS permissions, macOS permissions or network share permissions.
Check for BitLocker, FileVault or other encryption requiring a valid key or recovery credential.
For cloud or shared storage, confirm the user still has access to the correct account and folder.
Do not reset permissions recursively or take ownership of an entire drive without understanding the consequences.
For encrypted storage, do not format or initialise the volume while trying to regain access.
If the file exists and the issue is limited to authorised access, correct permissions through the appropriate administrator or account.

fixPermissions.title: Restore authorised access
body: Confirm the user has legitimate access to the file or storage.
Correct only the necessary file or folder permissions.
For network shares, check both share and filesystem permissions.
For encryption, use the correct account credentials or valid recovery key.
Avoid changing ownership or permissions on large unrelated folder trees.
Attempt to open the file again after restoring access.

checkFilesystemIssue.title: Check for filesystem or partition problems
body: Determine whether the volume is present but unreadable, unmounted or reporting an unsupported or RAW filesystem.
Check whether another computer can identify the drive without modifying its contents.
Check for a missing drive letter or mount point without formatting the volume.
If a drive appears unallocated, RAW or asks to be formatted, do not format or initialise it.
Avoid running write-capable repairs before protecting important data.
If the data is valuable, consider professional assessment or a non-destructive imaging workflow.
Only proceed with repair after the data has been secured and the consequences are understood.

stopUsingDrive.title: Stop using a suspected failing drive
body: Stop normal use of the affected drive immediately.
If the drive is clicking, repeatedly disconnecting or producing serious read errors, avoid further scanning.
Do not run CHKDSK, format, defragmentation, filesystem repair or repeated recovery scans on the failing source.
Do not reinstall the operating system onto the affected disk.
Power down safely if the data is critical or mechanical damage is suspected.
Assess whether a professional recovery service is needed before further attempts.
If the data is unimportant and backups are available, replace the faulty device instead.

storageRepairPlanning.title: Plan storage repair or replacement
body: The storage problem is not being treated as an active data recovery case.
Confirm that no required data remains on the affected volume before formatting, initialising or replacing it.
Use manufacturer diagnostics and appropriate repair procedures only after confirming data preservation.
If the drive is unreliable, replace it rather than trusting it with important new files.
Restore any required data from a verified backup.
Recheck drive health and backup configuration before returning the system to service.

replaceDrive.title: Replace the unreliable drive
body: The storage device is suspected of failure and the required data is backed up or no longer needed.
Replace the drive with a reliable storage device.
Restore required files from verified backups.
Do not reuse an unreliable drive for important data.
Confirm the replacement storage is operating correctly and backups are configured.

professionalRecovery.title: Professional data recovery recommended
body: The remaining recovery options are high risk or require specialised equipment.
Keep the original drive or storage device unchanged.
If physical failure is suspected, avoid further powering, scanning or repair attempts.
For valuable data, contact a professional recovery service and explain the device symptoms and previous actions.
Ask about assessment costs, handling procedures and recovery feasibility.
For encrypted drives, ensure valid credentials or recovery keys are available where required.
Do not format or overwrite the source before professional assessment.

recoverySuccessful.title: File recovered successfully
body: The required file has been recovered and verified.
Store the recovered copy in a safe, known location.
Open the file and confirm its contents are complete.
Create an additional backup separate from the original storage.
If cloud synchronisation caused the loss, review sync and deletion behaviour.
Configure a regular backup system to reduce the risk of future data loss.

recoveryUnsuccessful.title: No usable recovery found
body: The available recovery methods did not produce a usable copy.
Preserve the original storage if the data may be needed later.
Do not assume recovery is guaranteed through further software scans.
For SSDs, overwritten data and TRIM can prevent recovery.
If the information is valuable, professional assessment may still be appropriate.
Review backup coverage before returning the device to normal use.
